lenses.headline: The work built a list of leftovers for a problem the evidence says barely occurs (about 1.5% of runs, zero natural gaps), and skipped the gate the owner actually asked for. Freeze it, and spend the next effort on one real-feature trial of whether a second look after delivery finds anything a person would act on.

recommendations.claim: Cut the classified follow_on machinery down to a one-field handoff note ('what I would do next, and what answer I need'). Keep the request-file writer only if a person actually uses it.
recommendations.why: The shipped design has seven model-invented classes, evidence citations, a gate and a request-file generator. Your own data: decisions in 1.2% to 1.8% of 166 runs, no confirmed gap, and the one class that could run unattended (gap) appeared only when the request was written to produce it. A decision is by definition a request for a person, and the existing blocked/ask path already handles that. The classes add a model-judged taxonomy with no consumer. They also add surface area: three later test suites broke on hand-built handoff results, so every future handoff change pays for this.
recommendations.refuting_check: Take the 4 unprimed live runs plus 10 older finished runs. Replace follow_on with a free-text 'next' line. Ask the owner (blind to which format is which) to say which items he would act on. If the classified list surfaces actionable items the free text misses, keep the classes. Otherwise cut.
recommendations.cost: Low: about half a day, no model runs beyond re-reading existing handoffs

recommendations.claim: The owner's real goal is 'did the delivered feature actually meet intent, and what did building teach', and the gate that answers that was never built. Build the gate first, not the list.
recommendations.why: The dictated intention was a replanning step plus a gate that decides whether to re-enter. What shipped is a leftover list that never decides anything and never blocks 'done'. A leftover list depends on the building model volunteering its own shortfalls, so it only reports what the run already noticed. A gate that does not depend on the run's self-report (held-out acceptance, or a spec-vs-behaviour diff) catches what the run did not notice. The 166-run saturation (every run completes) also says the self-report path will mostly return nothing.
recommendations.refuting_check: On 10 finished runs, run a fresh-context reviewer that gets only the original request and the deployed behaviour (not the run's records) and produces acceptance probes. Count runs where a probe fails and a person agrees it is a real miss. If it finds roughly 0 in 10, the continuation idea is dead and the whole direction can be dropped with confidence.
recommendations.cost: Medium: one reviewer prompt and 10 model runs, about 1 to 2 days

recommendations.claim: Stop measuring on tiny arranged tasks and stop writing journal rounds about mechanics. The next evidence must come from one substantial feature on the owner's real work.
recommendations.why: Rounds 5 to 7 show the path works when primed. That was never in doubt, since it is a script writing a file. The questions that decide value (natural rate, whether a follow-on run repairs anything, whether the owner uses the command) are unmeasured, and each primed round adds journal and design-note weight (678 plus 925 lines) without answering them. The M3 tally script already exists; use it on real deliveries.
recommendations.refuting_check: Run the M3 tally over the owner's next 5 real deliveries. If a recommended run is started in 0 of 5 and the owner calls the list noise, treat the feature as unused and apply recommendation 1. If at least 2 of 5 are started and led to a change, keep it.
recommendations.cost: Low in effort but slow in calendar time (the next 5 deliveries)

recommendations.claim: The 'Determine how to conclude, plan out, and implement' loop is rewarding the session for shipping process rather than for a better product. Set a stop condition before further work on this direction.
recommendations.why: Two days produced 6 design-note revisions, 7 journal rounds, a release and a live check, for a thing whose measured demand was 1.2% to 1.8%. The session itself recorded that a replay advising to wait was 'evidence about demand that was not kept'. That is the pattern to avoid: each one-line prompt triggers more building, and the evidence against building was set aside. A pre-registered stop is cheap and honest.
recommendations.refuting_check: State in the journal: if the real-delivery tally (recommendation 3) shows under 1 in 5 deliveries with a recommended run actually started within 30 days, the feature is frozen and no further rounds are written. Check later whether that rule would have stopped Rounds 5 to 7.
recommendations.cost: Very low: one paragraph

recommendations.claim: If a continuation signal is wanted, take it from outside the run (failures and complaints after deployment, or the owner's own next prompt) rather than from the run's self-classification.
recommendations.why: The owner already sends a follow-up prompt after each delivery. That prompt is a free, high-quality label of 'what the delivery missed'. Logging it against the prior run's handoff (did the follow-up request correspond to any listed leftover?) measures the recall of the list without model-run cost and without priming. Low recall means the list is aimed at the wrong target.
recommendations.refuting_check: Take the owner's last 10 post-delivery prompts and the matching handoffs. If the handoff already listed the thing the owner asked for in at least 7 of 10, the list has value and my recommendation weakens. If under 3, it does not.
recommendations.cost: Low: manual read of about 10 pairs, about 1 hour

risks: Priming: all positive evidence (decision filed, gap filed, unattended run delivered) comes from requests written to produce that occasion, so it shows mechanics only and says nothing about natural use.

Small n and a single host/model/effort (Codex Terra xhigh on small command-line tasks); two to four runs per cell cannot support any rate claim, and the 166-run replay is saturated (every run completes), so it cannot show demand either way.

Model-written classes graded by the same model families: the reader passes (two of one model, one of another) share blind spots about what counts as a leftover, so the 1.2% to 1.8% may itself be unreliable in either direction.
Sunk-cost momentum: the owner's repeated one-line prompt plus a released feature makes stopping feel like a regression, so the direction may continue without evidence of demand.
Maintenance drag: the follow_on gate sits in the handoff path, and the sweep already broke three unrelated suites; every future handoff or test-fixture change must account for it.
Wrong target: a list that only the building model fills in cannot see what that model did not notice, which is the case that most matters for continuing a delivery.

lenses.headline: The built list answers "what did the run notice?", not "has the feature concluded?". A gate is only worth having if it fires on evidence the implementing model did not write and has been shown to fire on a known gap. Neither is true yet, so measure the gate's sensitivity on seeded gaps before building anything on top of it.

recommendations.claim: Before trusting any gate, calibrate it on seeded gaps that the request does not arrange. Take completed runs, silently break one requested outcome in the delivered build (drop it, weaken it, or hard-code a case) while the run's own tests stay green, then ask whether the gate fires. Do the same for the existing `follow_on` list as the baseline.
recommendations.why: The archive is saturated (26 of 26 brownfield runs pass every held-out check; `decision` in 1.2 to 1.8% of runs, no confirmed `gap`). The live cells were primed by requests that told the model to defer or reserve something, so they show the classifier obeys an arranged occasion, not that it detects a real gap. A gate with unmeasured recall can say 'concluded' on every run, and the original idea needs it to say 'not concluded' correctly. Seeding gives a known positive without waiting for the natural rate.
recommendations.refuting_check: Seed one gap in each of about 12 completed runs (3 kinds x 4 runs). If the model-classified `follow_on` list files a `gap` or `decision` for at least 10 of them with no prime, the list already is a sensitive gate and the rest of this critique is weaker. If it files 0 to 3 and an executable probe (rec 2) catches most, the list is a note-taker, not a gate.
recommendations.cost: About 12 to 24 model runs plus hand-seeding (1 to 2 days). No change to the product.

recommendations.claim: Replace the model-classified `gap` with an executable red: an independent reviewer pass (fresh context, a different model if possible) sees only the verbatim request and the running build, not the spec, lessons or self-reported leftovers. It must emit runnable black-box probes. Only a probe that fails against the delivered build counts as 'not concluded'. Prose findings go in as notes.
recommendations.why: The list is judged by the same context that built the feature, so it shares that context's blind spots. It also shares the request-to-spec drift, because the spec is the thing under suspicion. A failing probe is checkable by a script, is hard to game by relabelling, and has no class boundary to argue about. It turns the 'gap' versus 'note' coin-flip seen in the deferred-option cell into a pass or fail result.
recommendations.refuting_check: On the seeded set from rec 1 plus the same runs unseeded, compare the probe reviewer with the list. It is refuted if probes fail on more than about 10% of unseeded saturated runs (false alarms from over-reading the request), or catch no more seeded gaps than the list does.
recommendations.cost: One extra stage, one reviewer call plus probe execution per run (roughly 5 to 15 minutes, 1 model call; a modest slice of the run's token cost). Failure modes: probes that misread an ambiguous request and fail on a legitimate choice (those should go to `decision`, not `gap`), and flaky probes (run each twice).

recommendations.claim: Derive a ground-truth label from real history before designing the gate further. For each past owner delivery, mark it 'needed follow-up' if within N days there was a fix commit touching the delivered files, a revert, or an owner prompt like 'determine how to conclude', 'it does not work', 'also add'. Then score any candidate gate (the list, probes, reviewer) against that label.
recommendations.why: The owner's own next move is the real 'did building teach us something' signal, and it is free and already on disk. The current evidence has no label at all: classes are the system's own definitions, and E2E tasks are tiny and always complete. Real features are where 'not concluded' lives, and the natural rate of it there is the number that decides whether any of this is worth building.
recommendations.refuting_check: Take the last 20 to 30 real runs on the owner's repos. If fewer than about 10% have a follow-up within 14 days, there is little for a gate to catch and the direction should shrink to the lessons commit. If more than 30% do, the list's recall against that label can be computed immediately.
recommendations.cost: A few hours of read-only git and transcript mining, no model runs. Failure mode: follow-ups that are new scope, not gaps. Label by hand for the 20 or so positives.

recommendations.claim: Add a sealed acceptance check to ShipLoop itself. At test-strategy, a separate context writes acceptance checks from the request only, stored where the implementer and its loop never read them. They run once at release-verify or handoff. A pass means 'concluded on the request'. A failure that survives the in-run loop becomes a mandatory gap with an executable red. Keep it advisory for `done`.
recommendations.why: Production runs have no held-out check: the held-out checks exist only in the E2E apparatus. The implementer sees all its own tests, so test-passing is a weak proof of 'the request is met'. A sealed set breaks that coupling and costs one test run. Note the earlier decision that an end-of-run gate that refuses `done` has refused honest runs (the coverage-check replay); advisory use avoids repeating that.
recommendations.refuting_check: Replay on the seeded set (rec 1) and on 10 unseeded runs. It is refuted if sealed checks fail on honest unseeded runs more than about 10% of the time (they test a different reading of the request), or if they add nothing over the visible tests on the seeded gaps.
recommendations.cost: One extra authoring step plus one run of the checks. About 1 to 2 days to build, plus the replay. Failure modes: sealed checks that encode the author's reading, and a leaked path that lets the implementer see them (needs a guard).

recommendations.claim: Define 'concluded' as convergence, not as an empty list, and collapse the classes to what each action needs: executable red (start a run), person question (ask), and note. Only after rec 1 and rec 3 show a base rate above zero on real features, build the chain exit as 'two consecutive independent passes with no new red and no open decision'. Until then, cut auto-start, D3 chain machinery and the extension/debt/capability/person distinctions.
recommendations.why: An empty list from the same model is a statement of its own confidence, not a stopping rule. 'Two clean independent rounds' is the discipline the repo already uses elsewhere (review-converge) and has an exit that can be checked. Seven classes carry meaning only for the model that wrote them, and three of them ('person', 'capability', 'extension') are not different next actions. Complexity should follow a measured base rate, which is currently unmeasured.
recommendations.refuting_check: Count how often each class changes what the owner actually does in the next session (starts a run, answers, ignores). If the owner acts differently on 4 or more classes, the split is justified. If they act on 2, collapse it.
recommendations.cost: Cheap, mostly deletion and a count over existing evidence (under a day). Failure mode: collapsing classes loses a distinction that a later chain would need, which is recoverable from git.

risks: Circularity: the gate, its classes, and the cases that show it works were all produced by the same model family and session. A 'passing' live check shows the classifier follows a primed request, not that it detects an unprimed gap.

Saturation cuts both ways: the archive cannot show the value of a gate because everything completes, so success there says nothing. Do not read 'no gaps found in 166 runs' as 'the idea is not needed' either. The corpus cannot contain the thing being searched for.

Spec drift hides the gap: the spec, plan and tests all descend from one reading of the request. Any gate that reads those artifacts inherits that reading. Only a check that starts from the verbatim request, or from the owner's later behaviour, escapes it.

The deployed-feature signal does not exist for these runs: ShipLoop ends at handoff and observes nothing after it, so 'usage or failure signals' reduce to what the owner chooses to report, which is sparse and biased toward visible breakage. Use it as a label (rec 3), not as an automatic gate.

Sealed or independent checks can create false 'not concluded' signals when the request is ambiguous, which sends the owner more work than it saves. Route disputed readings to `decision`, and track the false-alarm rate as the primary cost.

Held-out checks and reviewers add cost on every run to catch something with a low natural rate. If rec 3 shows follow-ups under about 10%, the most valuable change may be to do nothing beyond the lessons commit.

lenses.headline: The target is probably wrong: the work classifies what a run says it left over, not whether the delivery matches what the requester wanted. The best alternatives measure that mismatch directly, starting with the owner's own post-delivery prompts as the ground-truth label, which is the cheapest step.

recommendations.claim: Use the owner's real post-delivery prompts as ground truth. For each delivery on a real feature (not E2E probes), record what the owner asked next (the repeated 'Determine how to conclude, plan out, and implement' plus any content they added or changed). Replay the follow_on list, or any candidate gate, against those deliveries and score it: would it have predicted that a follow-up was needed, and what it would be?
recommendations.why: The brief's evidence comes from 166 saturated E2E runs and 2 to 4 primed live runs; neither says whether the list matches anything the owner actually wanted. The owner's follow-up messages are the only natural label for 'not concluded'. The 'Determine how to conclude' prompt also suggests the owner wants a stop rule, which a leftovers list does not give.
recommendations.refuting_check: Take the last 10 to 20 real deliveries from session history. For each, mark 'owner asked for more' yes/no from the transcript. If the follow_on list (or the model's own handoff leftovers) predicts that mark no better than a coin flip, or the owner's next asks never correspond to a filed gap/decision, the leftovers direction is aimed at the wrong target.
recommendations.cost: Low: a few hours of reading transcripts and handoff results, no model runs.

recommendations.claim: Add a release-verification probe in a fresh context: from the verbatim original request only (not the spec, plan or tests the run wrote), a stage writes 3 to 5 acceptance checks and runs them against the delivered artifact as a new user would (README happy path, the request's literal wording, one adversarial input). Any failed or unrunnable check is a script-computed 'not concluded' signal.
recommendations.why: The run grades itself against a spec it wrote, so spec-versus-request drift is invisible to every current check. A held-out probe derived from the request breaks the shared-author blind spot and is a gate that does not depend on a model classifying its own leftovers. It is generic (no stack rules), consistent with the 'generic focus' decision.
recommendations.refuting_check: On 20 past E2E runs where the request is retained, run the probe and check whether it finds any defect or unmet request outcome that the run's own system-test missed. If it finds none in 20 on saturated runs, also run it on 5 runs with injected spec drift (a request clause quietly dropped from the spec). If it misses the injections, cut it.
recommendations.cost: Medium: one new stage prompt, plus about 25 runs of a single extra step; no harness changes needed for the offline replay.

recommendations.claim: Replace the model-classified 'gap' with a deterministic concluded test built from artifacts the run already holds: the coverage ledger and request requirements. Report, read-only and without gating, the count of request outcomes with no passing proof, unverified rows, and open assumptions. Show the raw rows rather than classes.
recommendations.why: The classes are the author's own, the model decides what counts as a leftover, and the only 'decision' class evidence is 2 of 166 (1.2% to 1.8%). A script-computed unmet-requirement count cannot be primed or flattered by wording. The earlier ledger work found an ID gate costs 25%, so use it only as a report, never as a gate.
recommendations.refuting_check: Compare the deterministic count to the model's follow_on on the same 20 to 40 runs. If the count is zero wherever the list is non-empty on real defects (or the reverse) the two disagree and one is wrong; hand-check 10 disagreements. If the count is always zero on saturated runs, it adds nothing there and should be tested on the real-feature set from recommendation 1.
recommendations.cost: Low to medium: a script over existing run records; no model calls.

recommendations.claim: Give the next intake an instrumented learning log instead of a new stage: keep the existing lessons ('open for the next run', 'key considerations'), but measure whether the next intake actually used each item (quoted, acted on, ignored). Prune what is never used and promote what is.
recommendations.why: The idea of 'what building taught' already exists as a lessons commit that the next run quotes. What is unknown is whether it changes behaviour. A reflection stage that adds a second list is cost with no evidence of use; usage evidence is the missing piece and is cheap to get from existing runs.
recommendations.refuting_check: In existing run pairs (run N and the next run on the same project), count lesson items quoted at intake and the share that appear in the next run's plan or spec. If under about 20% are used, a new reflection stage would not help either; if over 60%, extend the log rather than adding the follow-on machinery.
recommendations.cost: Low: offline trace reading over existing run records.

recommendations.claim: At the owner level, add a monthly review of follow-on outcomes with a kill criterion: how many printed follow-on commands the owner actually ran, how many ended in a delivery the owner accepted, and how many request files stayed unread. Retire the feature if fewer than about 1 in 5 are used over a fixed window, and write the stop rule for chains before D3's 'no ceiling' is exercised.
recommendations.why: The work has no adoption metric: nothing says the owner will ever run a printed command, and a person starts every follow-on. The original goal ('re-enter instead of exiting') implies a stop rule; D3 allows unbounded chains with no measure of when a chain should end, which risks endless low-value runs. A cadence with a kill metric keeps the direction honest.
recommendations.refuting_check: Count over the next 10 deliveries on real features how often a request file is generated and how often the owner uses it. If the owner never runs it (or reaches for 'Determine how to conclude' instead), the printed command adds nothing over what the owner already does.
recommendations.cost: Low: one counter in the run result plus a monthly 15-minute read.

risks: Wrong target: the intention is 'did building teach something that changes the spec or feature', but what was built is a self-reported leftover list. A run that says nothing is left cannot be told apart from a run that missed things.
The classifier and the thing classified are the same kind of model; the classes (gap, decision, person and so on) are the author's own, and readers agree only by one row on the decisive class.

Priming and arranged occasions: both positive live results used requests written to produce a decision or gap; unprimed runs produced notes only. The natural rate on real features is unmeasured, and the saturated E2E corpus cannot produce it.
Tiny n (0 to 4 runs per cell), one host and one model family at one effort level, so a stable-looking pass could be a lucky sample.
Goodhart on the list: once models know a gap triggers a request file, they may file notes to look compliant or file spurious gaps; nothing measures false positives against a held-out defect set.

Chains with no ceiling (D3) and no stop rule risk spending effort on low-value follow-ups, and the original 'gate' (has the feature concluded) was never built, so there is still no principled stopping point.

lenses.headline: Every number measures what a run chose to say about itself, so none can distinguish "nothing is left" from "the model did not notice". The cheapest high-value check is a hidden-probe recall test against deliveries whose true state is known independently of the model.

recommendations.claim: The central blind spot is the missing independent ground truth. The 166-run replay, the 4 unprimed live runs and the primed runs all score the model's own leftover text (read by readers of the same families). There is no measure of recall: how many real unmet outcomes a finished delivery contains versus how many the list names. 'No confirmed gap in 166 runs' and 'empty lists in unprimed runs' are therefore equally consistent with 'the system is complete' and 'the model does not look'. The journal's own flag of possible silence on seat-reservations (`[]` beside an open revalidation condition) is the visible edge of this.
recommendations.why: The E2E cases are saturated by construction: they complete when their own checks pass, so the corpus has almost no variance in delivery quality. A detector cannot be evaluated on a population where the positives are removed in advance. The conclusion 'gaps appear only when the request arranges them' (F49) is an artefact of that selection, not a finding about real features.
recommendations.refuting_check: Hold-out probes: for 4 to 6 existing cases, write 3 to 5 behavioural probes each for things a reasonable requester would expect but the request never states (tie rules, empty input, ordering, idempotence, error exit codes). Write them with a different model family from Terra, and write them BEFORE reading any run's follow_on or leftovers. Run them against retained final workspaces (the run folders under /Users/dadleet/e2e-runs hold run artefacts; confirm the product repos are retained, otherwise do 3 fresh --prompt runs per case with `--check` unchanged). If probes fail in about 15% or more of 'completed' runs while the lists name none of those failures, the reading 'few gaps exist' is refuted and the problem is recall. If fewer than 5% fail, the cut recommendation stands.
recommendations.cost: About 2 to 3 hours of one reader's time writing probes plus seconds of python per workspace if the products are retained; about 6 to 8 Terra xhigh runs at 12 to 20 minutes each if not. Offline version respects the owner's hold on live E2E cycles.

recommendations.claim: The live evidence for the build tests compliance with an arranged occasion, not detection. The requests that produced a decision or a gap said, in plain words, 'reserve this choice for the person' and 'build only the basic tool now and leave the option for later'. Any competent model files those. What the model did not do on its own: unprimed lists were 0, 1, 1, 0 entries, all notes.
recommendations.why: What the primed runs establish is mechanics: a printed command works, a request file blocks at spec and asks, an answered run delivers and does not re-file. That is useful as plumbing proof and says nothing about whether the list helps on the owner's real features. The reported 2 of 4 filing predictions (P3, P4 missed) are honest, but the write-up still reads the primed rounds as evidence for the direction.
recommendations.refuting_check: Run the same two primed requests with the occasion hidden in the world and not in the wording: a request whose second half is unsatisfiable in the sandbox (for example a behaviour that needs a capability the harness lacks) without the words 'later', 'defer' or 'reserve'. Score whether the list names it, by a script grep on the planted requirement's key phrase, not by a reader. Predict failure to file in 2 or more of 4; a pass refutes this claim.
recommendations.cost: 4 runs of 12 to 20 minutes, about 1 hour on Terra xhigh with the existing custom --prompt route; scoring is a script.

recommendations.claim: The classes and the gate are model-defined at both ends, so agreement between readers is not validity. The first reader, the three replay readers, and the subject that writes `follow_on` are all Claude or Codex frontier models given the same class definitions authored by the same session. Class counts of 1.2% to 1.8% decisions rest on one author's definition of 'decision' versus 'person' versus 'extension'.
recommendations.why: Inter-reader agreement shows the definitions are communicable, not that they carve the real distinction 'could this run unattended and be better?'. The distinction that matters for the intention (does a follow-on run change the delivered outcome?) is never labelled by anything outside the model. Redefining 'extension' or 'debt' by a few words moves the 'gap' count between 0 and several.
recommendations.refuting_check: Pre-register the class-to-outcome test: take the 25 non-empty leftovers from the peek and, for each, have a run (not a reader) attempt it unattended from the generated request; record whether the delivered product changes and passes an unchanged hidden check. If the per-class outcome (changed and verified) does not differ between 'gap' and 'extension'/'debt', the classes carry no decision value. Needs a case built for M2b, which the journal says still does not exist.
recommendations.cost: 25 follow-on runs is too many; do 6 (2 each from three classes), about 1.5 to 2 hours, after the probe experiment gives you something real to start from.

recommendations.claim: Single host, single model, single effort, tiny tasks, n of 2 to 4 per cell, so nothing here supports a rate or a transfer to the owner's real, larger features. 'Every run completes' is a property of Terra xhigh on cases written for E2E, not of ShipLoop.
recommendations.why: A list that is empty on a one-file CLI says little about a feature with several stages, shared state and a real deploy, where a leftover may be a behaviour the requester would call unfinished. Model choice is also known to move how much a run flags (K12 terms line, send-back excess in the journal's own history).
recommendations.refuting_check: Run the identical hidden-probe set (recommendation 1) with a different Claude host and model (the default Claude host, Sonnet) on 3 cases. If the lists' recall differs by more than 2 entries per case on the same planted failures, the list is model-specific and any rate is not a ShipLoop property.
recommendations.cost: 3 to 6 runs on the second host, about 1 to 1.5 hours; the `hosts.HOSTS` interface exists.

recommendations.claim: The cheapest decisive data about demand is the owner's own behaviour, and the work has not looked at it. The original intention was triggered by the owner's real experience after real deliveries; what the owner actually typed next (a repair, an extension, a clarification, nothing) is unprimed, unclassified-by-model ground truth about whether a follow-on run is needed and what it should contain.
recommendations.why: The follow-on build answered 'can a model file entries' (yes) and 'does the path work' (yes). The unmeasured, decisive quantity is P(owner sends a follow-up prompt after a delivery) and what kind it is. If most of the owner's follow-ups are corrections of behaviour the run delivered (gaps the list never named), that targets the probe and release-verify stage, not a leftover list. If they are mostly new ideas, the follow-on run is a convenience and the cut stands.
recommendations.refuting_check: From the session transcripts and ShipLoop request logs (read-only), take the last 20 real ShipLoop runs on the owner's own projects and the next owner message after each handoff; label by two readers blind to the follow_on design as repair, extension, question or none. Compare against what that run's lessons 'open for the next run' contained (past runs have it). If under 20% are repair or the lessons already named them, the recommend-only list is adequate; if over 40% are unnamed repairs, the list is aimed at a symptom.
recommendations.cost: About 1 hour of read-only analysis with `mcp__ccd_session_mgmt__search_session_transcripts` or the run folders; no model run.

risks: Reading the primed rounds (6 and 7) as support for auto-start or for the direction: they test plumbing; the journal itself says a gap appeared only when arranged, which the probe experiment may show is an artefact of unmeasured recall.

Same-family circularity: the subject, the first reader and the replay readers share class definitions written by this session; the agreement figures overstate how well classes capture real unmet need.
Selection: the corpus is saturated (every run completes), so absence of gaps in 166 runs is nearly guaranteed and carries almost no information about real features.

The unbuilt gate: what was built is a list of leftovers, not the owner's gate 'has the feature concluded?'. Further rounds on the list refine an instrument that never answers the owner's actual question; a held-out acceptance check does answer it.

Sunk-cost drift: seven journal rounds and a release now make the feature feel established; the cheap kill criterion (hold-out probes fail and the list misses them, or the owner's follow-ups are mostly unnamed repairs) should be set before reading the results.

Cost of the E2E harness: runs of 12 to 20 minutes each on a heavily loaded machine (load 50 to 87 noted in the journal) and the owner's hold on live cycles make a live-run-first plan slow; the offline hidden-probe check is the way to avoid that.

recommendations.claim: Use the owner's own next message after each real delivery as the ground-truth label for 'not concluded'. Score the follow_on list (and any candidate gate) against it before building anything more.
recommendations.why: All four lenses raised this. The 166-run replay and the primed live runs only measure what a run says about itself. The owner's follow-up prompt is the one unprimed signal that the delivery missed something. It is also the only way to measure whether the list names what the owner actually asked for next.
recommendations.refuting_check: Take the last 10 to 20 real deliveries and the matching handoffs. Label the owner's next message as repair, extension, question or none, ideally with readers blind to the follow_on design. If the handoff already named the follow-up in about 7 of 10, the list has value. If it named under about 3 of 10, or follows no better than a coin flip, the list is aimed at the wrong target. Write the thresholds in the journal before reading the results.
recommendations.cost: Low. A few hours of read-only transcript and git mining, no model runs. Failure mode: follow-ups that are new scope rather than gaps, so hand-label the positives.

recommendations.claim: Measure the list's recall on gaps the request did not arrange: seed one known gap into each of about 12 completed runs while their own tests stay green, then see whether follow_on files it.
recommendations.why: The archive is saturated, since every run completes, so it contains no positives. The primed live cells show the model obeys an arranged occasion, not that it detects an unnoticed gap. Without a recall figure, 'no confirmed gap in 166 runs' and 'the model does not look' cannot be told apart.
recommendations.refuting_check: Seed gaps of 3 kinds across 4 runs each, silently dropping, weakening or hard-coding a requested outcome, and score the filed follow_on entries by script. If the unprimed list files a gap or decision for at least 10 of 12, it is already a sensitive gate and this critique weakens. If it files 0 to 3, it is a note-taker.
recommendations.cost: Medium. About 12 to 24 model runs plus hand-seeding, 1 to 2 days. No product change.

recommendations.claim: Build the 'did the delivery meet the request' check the owner actually described, as a fresh-context probe stage. It sees only the verbatim request and the running build, writes 3 to 5 runnable acceptance probes, and only a failing probe counts as 'not concluded'. Keep it advisory.
recommendations.why: The current list depends on the building model volunteering its own shortfalls. The spec, plan and tests all descend from one reading of the request, so spec-versus-request drift is invisible to every current check. A probe that starts from the verbatim request is script-checkable and escapes that shared reading. It also turns the gap versus note coin-flip into pass or fail. Keep it advisory because an end-of-run gate that refuses done has refused honest runs before (the coverage-check replay).
recommendations.refuting_check: Run it on the seeded set from recommendation 2, on about 10 to 20 unseeded finished runs, and on a few runs with a request clause quietly dropped from the spec. It is refuted if probes fail on more than about 10% of honest runs, which are false alarms from over-reading the request, or if it catches no more seeded gaps than the list does. Disputed readings should route to decision, not gap.
recommendations.cost: Medium. One reviewer prompt plus probe execution, about 1 to 2 days to build, and one extra call per run afterwards.

recommendations.claim: Set a pre-registered stop rule now, and collect the natural rate from the owner's next 5 real deliveries with the existing M3 tally on one substantial feature, not on more tiny arranged tasks.
recommendations.why: The decisive quantities are unmeasured: the natural rate, whether a recommended run is ever started, and whether the owner uses the printed command. Rounds 5 to 7 only proved the plumbing works when primed. Two days produced 6 design-note revisions, 7 journal rounds and a release for a measured demand of 1.2% to 1.8%, and the evidence against building was set aside. A written stop condition counters that momentum.
recommendations.refuting_check: Write the rule in the journal first. If under 1 in 5 deliveries within 30 days has a recommended run actually started, the feature is frozen and no further rounds are written. Later check whether that rule would have stopped Rounds 5 to 7.
recommendations.cost: Very low to write, one paragraph. Slow in calendar time, because the tally needs the next 5 deliveries.

recommendations.claim: Run the unprimed-occasion test: repeat the two primed requests with the occasion built into the world, such as an unsatisfiable second half in the sandbox, and without the words 'later', 'defer' or 'reserve'. Score filing by script grep on the planted phrase.
recommendations.why: The decision and gap results came from requests that told the model to defer or reserve something, so they show compliance with an arranged occasion. The 4 unprimed runs produced 0, 1, 1, 0 entries, all notes. This directly tests whether detection exists without priming.
recommendations.refuting_check: Predict failure to file in at least 2 of 4 runs. Filing in all 4 refutes this claim.
recommendations.cost: Low. 4 runs of 12 to 20 minutes on the existing custom prompt route, and scoring is a script.

recommendations.claim: Do not collapse or cut the classes on opinion. Count whether each class changes what the owner does next (starts a run, answers, ignores). Collapse to executable red, person question and note if the owner acts differently on 2 or fewer classes.
recommendations.why: Seven model-invented classes graded by the same model families carry meaning only for the model that wrote them. Three of them (person, capability, extension) are not different next actions. Reader agreement shows the definitions are communicable, not that they are valid. The lenses differ on timing, so this deliberately waits for the owner-action data from recommendation 1.
recommendations.refuting_check: From the real-delivery data, list each filed item and the owner's action. If the owner acts differently on 4 or more classes, the split is justified. If on 2, collapse. Fall back to the one-field handoff note only if the classified list surfaces nothing the free-text note misses on the 4 unprimed plus about 10 older runs (the owner reads blind to format).
recommendations.cost: Low. Mostly counting existing evidence, under a day. Deletion is recoverable from git.

recommendations.claim: Add a read-only, non-gating script report from artifacts the run already holds: request outcomes with no passing proof, unverified ledger rows and open assumptions, shown as raw rows rather than classes.
recommendations.why: A script-computed count cannot be primed or flattered by wording, and it gives a cross-check on the model's list at no model cost. It must stay a report, because the earlier ledger work found an ID gate costs 25%.
recommendations.refuting_check: Compare the count with follow_on on the same 20 to 40 runs and hand-check 10 disagreements. If the count is always zero on saturated runs, it adds nothing there. Re-test it on the real-feature set from recommendation 1.
recommendations.cost: Low to medium. A script over existing run records, no model calls.

disagreements: Cut now or wait for data. The cut lens wants the classified machinery reduced to a one-field handoff note now. The gate lens wants classes collapsed but the convergence exit built only after a base rate above zero shows up. The evidence lens says the cut stands only if hidden probes fail in under about 5% of runs. The ideas lens wants a monthly review with a kill criterion rather than an immediate cut. This is recorded as unresolved, and recommendation 6 defers it to the owner-action data.

Thresholds differ and were not reconciled. The 'list has value' bar is 7 of 10 (cut) versus better than a coin flip (ideas) versus under 20% repairs (evidence). The false-alarm bar for probes is above about 10% (gate, ideas) versus 15% or more of runs with unnamed failures as proof that recall is the problem (evidence). Pre-register one set before reading any results.

Blocking or advisory. The cut lens says build 'the gate' the owner asked for. The gate lens says keep it advisory for done, citing the earlier coverage-check refusals. The ideas lens says report only, without gating. The merged list takes advisory, but the cut lens did not endorse that.
Scale of the probe-stage cost. The cut lens estimates 1 to 2 days and 10 runs. The ideas lens estimates about 25 replay runs, and the gate lens adds seeded runs. Total cost is therefore uncertain.

Value of the primed live rounds. Cut and evidence read them as plumbing proof only, with no demand evidence. Gate treats them as showing the classifier follows an arranged request. None argues they support the direction, so there is no real conflict, but the cut lens would stop writing such rounds while the evidence lens would still run one more unprimed variant (recommendation 5).
stop_doing: Writing further journal rounds and design-note revisions on primed or arranged tasks. They only show the mechanics work.
Reading the 166-run saturated corpus as evidence either that demand is low or that it is high. It has no positives by construction.
Treating agreement between same-family readers on the model's own class definitions as validity.
Building auto-start, D3 unbounded chains or finer class distinctions before any natural base rate exists.
Letting the owner's repeated one-line prompt plus a released feature stand in for evidence of demand.
synthesis.next_step: Write the pre-registered thresholds and the stop rule into the journal. Then mine the owner's last 10 to 20 real post-delivery messages against the matching handoffs, labeling each as repair, extension, question or none. This needs no model runs and a few hours of work, and its result decides whether recommendations 2, 3 and 6 go ahead.
